tagline: An angler with a worm on a stick and a lightning gulp
summary: A lumpy, slow-moving anglerfish that sits motionless on the seabed, blending in, while it twitches a lure made from its first dorsal fin spine. When curious prey comes close, the frogfish's mouth snaps open and sucks it in within milliseconds — even prey nearly twice its own size.

stats.size: Commonly about 10 cm; up to about 25 cm
stats.depth: From under 1 m to over 200 m; often around 40 m
stats.range: Tropical and warm-temperate Atlantic and Indo-Pacific waters
stats.diet: Fishes and other small animals drawn in by its lure

facts.title: A fin turned fishing rod
facts.text: Its front-most dorsal fin spine has become a rod, the illicium, tipped with a bait called the esca. In this species the esca bears 2–7 worm-like appendages that wriggle like tempting prey.

facts.title: Gone in six milliseconds
facts.text: Its jaws open so suddenly that prey is sucked in along with water in about six milliseconds. High-speed filming has shown frogfishes have one of the fastest feeding mechanisms of any vertebrate.

facts.title: Eyes bigger than its stomach
facts.text: A huge mouth and stretchy stomach let it swallow prey up to twice its own size.

facts.title: Slow-motion chameleon
facts.text: Its colour is extremely variable, and over a few weeks a striated frogfish can completely change colour to match its surroundings.

facts.title: Eggs on a raft
facts.text: Its eggs are released wrapped in a ribbon-like, floating mass of mucus known as an 'egg raft'.

references.title: High-speed cinematographic evidence for ultrafast feeding in antennariid anglerfishes (Grobecker & Pietsch 1979, Science)

image.caption: A 'hairy' striated frogfish on black sand in Lembeh Strait, Indonesia
image.creator: Manuae

gallery.caption: The rod and lure in profile: a striated frogfish from the Gulf of Mexico (NOAA)

notes: Chose Antennarius striatus (striated/hairy frogfish) — commonName changed to 'Striated Frogfish'; rename to plain 'Frogfish' if the group name is preferred. The hero shows the long-filamented 'hairy' form, which is A. striatus (FishBase notes males have more extended skin appendages). Gallery is a live NOAA specimen photographed in a tank (some glass reflections visible). The 6 ms figure is from the Florida Museum; Grobecker & Pietsch 1979 (ref 3) is the original high-speed film study.
